html:
A large silver coin first struck around 1518 at Joachimsthal, a mining town in Bohemia, now Jáchymov in the Czech Republic. A rich silver strike there in 1516 let the local Schlick family mint big coins in great numbers.

People shortened the name to "thaler" (from Tal, valley). The coin set a pattern: across the Holy Roman Empire and beyond, large silver coins of about the same size were called thalers for three centuries. In Dutch it became "daalder", and English speakers turned that into "dollar".

The word then moved to the Spanish silver peso, the Spanish dollar, minted from American silver such as Potosí. It was so common in the British colonies that the United States named its own coin the dollar in 1792.

Joachimsthal had a second life later. The waste from its mines held uranium ore, and Marie Curie used it to find radium.
